blocks.text: 1. Partial Dependence Plots
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354498-35529607.png

SHAP and LIME, the two previous topics, both focused on explaining one specific, individual prediction at a time, exactly how much each feature contributed to that one particular case. Partial Dependence Plots step back to a broader, more aggregate question instead: as one specific feature varies across its range, how does the model's prediction change on average, across the entire dataset?

This directly connects back to the global feature importance view already covered for both SHAP and Permutation Importance, though Partial Dependence Plots go further, revealing not just how much a feature matters overall, but the actual specific shape of that feature's relationship with the model's predictions.
2. The Core Mechanism
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354498-310650215.png

Building a Partial Dependence Plot for one specific feature, house square footage for instance, starts by picking a range of test values to examine for that feature, perhaps 500 through 5000 square feet in reasonable increments. For each individual test value in this range, that feature's actual value gets replaced with this same test value across every single row in the entire dataset, regardless of what that row's true, original square footage actually was.

The model then predicts on this entire modified dataset, and all of the resulting predictions get averaged together into one single number for that specific test value. Plotting the test value on the X-axis against this averaged prediction on the Y-axis, repeated across every test value in the chosen range, produces the final Partial Dependence Plot, a direct visualization of how the model's average prediction responds as this one feature moves across its range.
3. Isolating One Feature's Marginal Effect
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354498-595244750.png

This directly connects back to the ceteris paribus, all-else-equal, interpretation already covered for Multiple Linear Regression's coefficients in the Regression module. A Partial Dependence Plot isolates exactly one feature's marginal effect on the model's predictions, while holding every other feature's actual, real, observed distribution constant across the entire dataset, rather than fixing those other features at some single, arbitrary value.

This shows directly how the model's prediction responds specifically to this one feature, averaged fairly over the genuine, real variation that exists in every other feature across the dataset, giving a considerably more representative picture of that one feature's true marginal effect than examining a single, arbitrary example alone ever could.
4. Reading the Plot's Shape
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354499-491401632.png

The overall shape of a Partial Dependence Plot carries direct, interpretable meaning. A rising line indicates that higher values of the examined feature are associated with higher average predictions, while a falling line indicates the opposite relationship, higher feature values associated with lower average predictions.

A flat line indicates the feature has little to no meaningful average effect on the model's predictions at all, information genuinely worth knowing about a feature's practical relevance. A curved, non-linear shape reveals that the feature's effect actually changes across its own range, rather than following one simple, constant relationship throughout, a genuinely richer signal than a single, fixed importance score could ever convey on its own.

blocks.text: 5. Revealing Non-Linear Relationships

This connects directly back to Polynomial Regression, and to tree-based models generally, both already covered throughout the Regression and Classification modules. Plain Linear Regression coefficients, already covered in depth in their own topic, can only ever describe a straight-line, constant relationship between a feature and the prediction, since that is the fundamental shape a linear model is capable of representing at all.

A Partial Dependence Plot can reveal a genuinely curved, non-linear relationship directly, regardless of what kind of model actually produced it, tree-based ensemble, kernel-based SVM, or otherwise, since it works purely by observing the model's actual predictions across a range of test values rather than by reading any internal coefficient at all. This is a real, practical advantage over relying on coefficients alone, particularly for any model type capable of capturing non-linear relationships, exactly the kind of algorithm covered throughout much of the Classification and Ensemble Learning modules.
6. The Two-Feature Version
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444354499-106414794.png

A Partial Dependence Plot can also be built for two features simultaneously, varying both features together across a grid of their combined values, rather than examining just one feature in isolation the way the standard version covered so far in this topic does.

This two-feature version reveals interaction effects directly: whether one feature's impact on the prediction genuinely depends on the other feature's value too, rather than each feature contributing its own separate, independent effect. Since this involves two varying dimensions instead of one, the result is typically visualized as a heatmap or a full three-dimensional surface, rather than the simple two-dimensional line used for a single feature, directly showing how the two features jointly shape the model's predictions together.
7. A Genuine Weakness: Unrealistic Combinations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444355247-46941449.png

It is worth connecting this directly back to the exact correlated-feature weakness already covered in depth for Permutation Importance in its own topic. Setting one feature to an artificial test value while holding every other feature fixed at its own real, original values, exactly the mechanism covered earlier in this topic, can create genuinely unrealistic feature combinations that would rarely or never occur in real, actual data.

A house dataset might, for instance, end up temporarily assigning 10 bedrooms to a row whose square footage remains at a typical small-home value, an artificial, unrealistic combination the real world essentially never produces. The resulting Partial Dependence Plot reflects the model's behavior on these artificial combinations, which may not accurately represent how that model would genuinely behave on realistic, naturally occurring data, a real, important caveat to keep in mind when interpreting results.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This weakness matters most when the feature being examined is strongly correlated with other features in the dataset, exactly the same correlation concern already covered for Permutation Importance, since strong correlation makes artificial, unrealistic combinations considerably more likely to arise during the plot's construction.

blocks.text: 8. Complementary, Not Competing, with Local Techniques

blocks.alt: Complementary, Not Competing, with Local Techniques
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444355249-428186831.png

It is worth summarizing the relationship to SHAP and LIME, both covered in the previous two topics, directly. SHAP and LIME explain one specific, individual prediction, revealing exactly how each feature contributed to that one particular case. Partial Dependence Plots instead show one feature's average effect across the entire dataset, a genuinely complementary, rather than competing, kind of insight.

These two kinds of explanation are best used together in practice: individual-prediction explanations from SHAP or LIME to understand specific, particular cases, combined with an overall, aggregate Partial Dependence Plot to understand a feature's general, dataset-wide behavior pattern, giving a genuinely complete picture that neither approach alone could fully provide.

blocks.text: 9. When Partial Dependence Plots Are the Right Choice

Partial Dependence Plots are the right choice specifically when understanding a feature's overall relationship with the model's predictions matters, rather than just explaining one single instance, a genuinely different, complementary question from what SHAP or LIME, both covered in their own topics, are built to answer.

They are also the right choice for communicating model behavior visually to a non-technical audience, since a simple line or curve is often considerably more immediately accessible than a table of individual SHAP values would be. And they are directly useful for checking whether a model has correctly captured an expected, genuine real-world relationship, confirming directly, for instance, that a larger house genuinely predicts a higher price as intuitively expected, a sanity check worth running on any model before trusting its predictions in a genuinely consequential setting.
10. Worked Example
The example below computes and inspects a Partial Dependence Plot for a single feature, directly examining how the model's average prediction changes as that feature varies.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.uniform(500, 5000, size=(300, 2))  # feature 0: square footage, feature 1: age
y = 50000 + 150 * X[:, 0] - 800 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(scale=20000, size=300)

model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)

pd_result = partial_dependence(model, X, features=[0], grid_resolution=10)
test_values = pd_result['grid_values'][0]
averaged_predictions = pd_result['average'][0]

print("Square footage | Average predicted price")
for value, prediction in zip(test_values, averaged_predictions):
    print(f"  {value:.0f} sq ft: ${prediction:,.0f}")

print("\nNotice the average prediction rises consistently as square footage increases, confirming the expected relationship")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The rising pattern in average predicted price as square footage increases directly confirms the model correctly captured the expected, genuine real-world relationship, exactly the sanity-checking use case covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Partial Dependence Plots show how a model's average prediction changes as one feature varies, across the entire dataset.
They isolate one feature's marginal effect, holding every other feature's real distribution constant, echoing ceteris paribus.
A rising, falling, flat, or curved shape each carry distinct, directly interpretable meaning about a feature's relationship.
They reveal genuinely non-linear relationships directly, a real advantage over reading coefficients alone.
A two-feature version reveals interaction effects, visualized as a heatmap or 3D surface.
Setting features to artificial test values can create unrealistic combinations, a genuine weakness echoing Permutation Importance's correlation concern.
They are complementary, not competing, with SHAP and LIME, best used together for both individual and aggregate views.
They fit understanding overall feature relationships, visual communication, and sanity-checking expected real-world patterns.
Next up: ICE Plots, which reveal individual-instance versions of the same relationship a Partial Dependence Plot averages together.
